title: The five fires (5.4–5.9)
hook: a king asks a proud young scholar five questions he can't answer, and the answer turns out to be the whole cycle of life told as five fires
carry: rain to food to seed to person

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upakosala and the fires, the student who tended them for twelve years. Your line was the teacher within. Did you pause and ask yourself first? Day three hundred thirty-eight.

A young man named Shvetaketu walks into the court of a king, Pravahana Jaivali, freshly educated and very sure of himself. The king asks: has your father taught you? Yes, sir. Then do you know where people go when they leave this world? No. How they come back? No. Why that other world never fills up? No. Five questions, five blanks. Shvetaketu storms home to his father: you told me I was educated! His father, a famous teacher, admits he doesn't know either. So the father goes to the king himself and asks to be taught. And what the king teaches him is a picture of five fires.
screen: `FIVE QUESTIONS, FIVE BLANKS.` → `THE FATHER DOESN'T KNOW EITHER.` → `HE GOES TO THE KING.`

segments.voice: Picture the sacrifice you met at the start of the week: a fire, and an offering poured into it. Now the king says: the whole world works like that. Five fires, five offerings. The first fire is the sky world up there. The gods pour in faith, and out of it comes Soma, the moon. The second fire is the rain cloud. Soma is poured in, and out comes rain. The third fire is the earth. Rain is poured in, and out comes food: rice, barley, plants. The fourth fire is a man. Food is poured in, and out comes seed. The fifth fire is a woman. Seed is poured in, and out comes a child. Then the king says the line the whole passage rests on: in the fifth offering, the waters come to be called a person. Follow it once more. Rain to food to seed to person. You are, in this picture, weather that has been offered and transformed five times. And it doesn't stop at birth. The person lives, dies, and is placed on the funeral fire, the last fire, and the cycle turns again. The next chapter describes the paths the dead take from there, the way of the gods and the way of the ancestors. Notice two things. First, a king, a warrior, is teaching a priest; the text has the king say this knowledge had not gone to brahmins before. Second, the fire is everywhere: not only on the altar, but in clouds, soil, bodies and births. The ritual became a way to see the whole world.
screen: `THE KING'S FIVE FIRES.` · `SKY, CLOUD, EARTH, MAN, WOMAN.` · `THE WATERS BECOME A PERSON.` · `A KING TEACHES A PRIEST.` · then, large: `RAIN TO FOOD TO SEED TO PERSON.`

segments.voice: Today's practice follows the water. Sit and settle. Breathe in, and think of rain falling somewhere far away. Breathe out. Breathe in, and think of a field, a grain of rice, a vegetable, fed by that rain. Breathe out. Breathe in, and think of a meal that became part of your body. Breathe out. Then simply feel your body sitting here, made, the king would say, of offered rain. The bell holds the time.
The five fires. Sky, rain cloud, earth, man and woman, each one receiving an offering and giving something new, until the waters become a person.
Your line: rain to food to seed to person. Today, at one meal, think for a moment of the rain that's in it. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Hindu rites of passage, from conception to cremation, are traditionally performed around a sacred fire, and many Hindus understand cremation as a final offering into the fire.

original.note: Sanskrit pañcāgni: pañca, five, + agni, fire. the five fires through which the waters pass to become a person.

trapdoor: what you thought: five sacred fires on an altar.
what it means: the whole cycle of life as a sacrifice: sky, cloud, earth, man, woman, each a fire turning one thing into the next.
what a scholar hears: the panchagni-vidya, Chandogya 5.3–5.10 (paralleled in Brihadaranyaka 6.2), one of the oldest Indian accounts of rebirth, taught by a kshatriya king.

notes: The king's questions are compressed: the script names three of the five (5.3.2–3). Confirm the paraphrase.
In 5.3.7 the king says this knowledge had not gone to brahmins before; the script reports that without commentary. Confirm tone.
Five fires: yonder world (faith → King Soma), Parjanya (Soma → rain), earth (rain → food), man (food → seed), woman (seed → embryo). Confirm 'Soma, the moon' identification.
Shvetaketu's father is Gautama (Uddalaka Aruni), who appears by name tomorrow.
